URL: https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2026/sep/26/labour-must-reunite-progressive-voters-to-win-the-next-election-says-lucy-powell
Guardian — published 2026-09-26T05:00:29Z = 06:00 BST Sat 26 Sep 2026. By Jessica Elgot.

HEADLINE: Labour must reunite progressive voters to win the next election, says Lucy Powell
Standfirst: The deputy leader wants the party to take advantage of a split on the right and not be embarrassed to show its values

FACTS:
- Lucy Powell is Labour's deputy leader (won the race 12 months ago) and Education Secretary.
- She says Labour must "reunite the progressive voter coalition" to take advantage of a split on the right and win the next election.
- She said the party had clearly required a "change of leader" to revive its fortunes and tell a better story, after becoming "too technical and pessimistic".
- Burnham rejected snap-election speculation on Friday and said the next contest would be in 2029.
- "the Labour conference will get underway this weekend with polls beginning to show for the first time in almost two years that Labour might be within touching distance of winning a majority at the next election - 12 months on from polls that suggested Reform UK could win a huge victory."
- NEW POLICY: Ahead of her conference speech, Powell said she will use her new role to announce AN EXPANSION OF ANTI-HARASSMENT WORK IN SCHOOLS. She will say schools must go further than the strategy announced earlier this year to tackle misogyny, where pupils will learn about deepfakes, image-based abuse and online harassment. Schools would be required to "embed healthy relationships and belonging into every part of school life, not just RSHE [relationships, sex and health education] lessons" and show they were helping to create real-world, authentic community.
- Powell declined to agree directly with chancellor John Healey that Burnham's government was offering "continuity".
- Powell wants to use the social media ban for under-16s as a moment to think about how to help young people build real-life communities.

QUOTE (Lucy Powell, Labour deputy leader and Education Secretary): "If you look at the evidence from recent elections - right across the board - it's clear that whichever party manages to unite its voter coalition is the one that wins. And for us on the left, that means bringing our centre-left bloc back together." She added that "includes some who have considered Reform as they have lost faith in the status quo".

QUOTE (Lucy Powell): "I've always thought there was a clear majority in this country who didn't want the kind of politics of Reform and that divisive blaming of others - they didn't like it."

QUOTE (Lucy Powell): "The challenge has been that sentiment has not all come to Labour and the progressive coalition was very, very fragmented. And part of our task and challenge is to reunite that progressive alliance and that voter coalition. I think we can. We've got red shoots of hope coming through."

QUOTE (Lucy Powell, on misogyny in schools): "We simply cannot just teach our way out of misogyny. Schools with strengthened RSHE teaching but no wider culture shift will not shift attitudes."

QUOTE (Lucy Powell, on Labour values): "Let's not be embarrassed about that, that's what we are. We lift children out of poverty, we take the difficult decisions in order to do that. I think at times we've been a bit worried about the reaction rather than just being clear about why we're doing that."

QUOTE (Lucy Powell): "There was a real strong desire for that clearer political communication. Of purpose, of story, of values. Andy knew that that's what he needed to do. That was what the moment required."

QUOTE (Lucy Powell, on welfare): "If we're not for pensioner poverty, and we're not addressing that, and we are not supporting people who need the safety net, then what are we for?" She added the government under Starmer had "lost sight of some of the politics and the purpose" once in power.

QUOTE (Lucy Powell): "It's really encouraging to see that people are coming back. Andy's shown that we can win in places like Makerfield against Reform, and in some key council byelections we previously lost to the Greens in May."
